The achievement I am most proud of is giving a TEDx talk in high school on gender equality in education. Addressing a large audience on a topic I cared about meant stepping well beyond my comfort zone, managing self-doubt, and building skills I still draw on.

Preparation was demanding. Over several weeks I researched, wrote, and rehearsed so the argument was persuasive and delivery assured. Fitting that work around academic and extracurricular commitments tested my organisation and time management under pressure. Constructive comments in rehearsals often required substantial rewrites; those iterations taught resilience and the habit of adapting to improve rather than defending a first draft.

On the day itself I confronted nerves directly. Experience as President of my school’s Debate Society and as Chair of the Cambridge Model United Nations helped me stay composed and audience-focused, drawing on public-speaking practice I had already built. On stage I concentrated on communicating clearly and persuasively, aiming to prompt critical thought about education’s role in advancing gender equality.

Delivering the talk successfully was a personal milestone and a chance to start meaningful conversations on an issue that matters to me. The process strengthened confidence, resilience, and communication under pressure—capabilities I expect to rely on in a legal career. I am proud of it because sustained effort and determination created an opportunity for real impact.
